Abstract
        

The balanced chromatic number of a signed graph G^\widehat{G} is the minimum number of balanced sets that cover all vertices of GG. Studying structural conditions which implies bound on the balanced chromatic number of signed graphs then is among the most fundamental problems in graph theory. In this work, we initiate the study of coloring hereditary classes of signed graphs. Considering the class of complete graphs, any such set FF must also contain a complete graph. Gyárfás and Sumner, independently, conjectured, in [7] and [14], that any such pair is enough for Forbi​n​d⁡(F)\Forb_{ind}{(F)} to have a bounded chromatic number:



Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture.



For any forest FF and any complete graph KtK_{t} the class Forbi​n​d⁡{F,Kt}\Forb_{ind}{\{F,K_{t}\}} has a bounded chromatic number.





The goal of this work is to consider potential extensions of this conjecture and related results to the class of signed graphs. To this end, we first introduce the notions and concepts.




1.1 Definitions and Notations




A signed graph is a pair (G,σ)(G,\sigma) where GG is a graph and σ:E⁡(G)→{+,−}\sigma:E(G)\to\{+,-\} is a mapping that assigns to each edge one of the two signs: positive or negative. If Σ\Sigma is the set of negative edges, then (G,σ)(G,\sigma) can be equivalently presented as (G,Σ)(G,\Sigma). When σ\sigma is of little importance, we may write G^\widehat{G} in the place of (G,σ)(G,\sigma). The subgraph (V⁡(G),Σ)(V(G),\Sigma) of G^\widehat{G} is denoted by G^−\widehat{G}^{-}.




The graph GG is the underlying graph of G^\widehat{G}. A pair of parallel edges of different signs is called a digon. However, unless especially mentioned, in the rest of this work, we only consider signed simple graphs.




Switching a vertex vv of (G,σ)(G,\sigma) is to multiply the sign of each edge incident to vv by −-. Observe that switching is an involution, and that the order doesn’t matter when switching multiple vertices. Therefore, we may switch a set of vertices, meaning that we switch all of the vertices of the set in an arbitrary order.
